extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of Japanese theatre/cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and evaluative account of traditional Japanese Nō (No) theatre: its aesthetics, personnel, music, stage conventions, structure, and moral/religious functions, intended to explain what constitutes a proper or characteristic Nō performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nō chief feature — exclusive connection with ideal beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Nō performance is a very simple kind of dance, whose chief feature is its exclusive connection with ideal beauty, wholly regardless of any decorations on the stage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic principle: emphasis on ideal/spiritual beauty over realistic stage decoration; the performance should invite and cultivate a trained imagination rather than rely on literal scenery. The quoted authority links this to the ‘suggestion of spiritual ideals to a trained and sympathetic imagination’ as the controlling artistic principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal, suggestive stage decoration (pine-tree motif)
rubrics_metrics.description: The painted pine-tree on the back wall is meant only to suggest the original outdoor setting; rudely made props may be placed but are intended to represent almost anything (a mound, mountain, house, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage properties must be minimal and symbolic; their chief aim is to call up the original to the imagination of the audience rather than to depict literal scenery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement and gesture mediated by the folding fan
rubrics_metrics.description: “The movements of the performer, in most cases, are likewise simple and entirely dependent upon the flourishes of a folding fan in his hand, for the expression of their natural beauty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors should use highly conventionalized fan gestures to convey action and emotion; large, literal gestures are inappropriate—expression is stylized through fan work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion and expression should be suggested, not declaimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Any emotion of the part played is not studiously expressed by external motions and appearances, but is suggested rather than proclaimed; ideas and emotions are suggested rather than declaimed by natural gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestion is subtle and follows conventional rules; only a highly instructed audience can fully decode the intended ideas and emotions. Avoid overt emoting—preference for restraint and implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventionalized, carefully adapted acting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestion of ideas and emotions is ‘so subtly done and so carefully adapted to conventional rules’ that only the most highly instructed of the audience can fully understand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting must adhere to traditional conventions and codified gestures; evaluation of excellence depends on fidelity to those conventions and on the performer’s subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of comic element (Kyogen) from serious/religious pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic element (Kyogen) is kept separate from the religious, and thus is never allowed to disturb or degrade the ethical impressions and teachings of the main dramatic performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming and tonal control: Kyogen interludes provide relief but must not intrude on the moral/spiritual seriousness of main Nō pieces; judges of authenticity look for this clear separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-day program structure: at least five numbers of different kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete Nō performance should last through an entire long day, and should consist of not fewer than five numbers, each of a different kind; the serious pieces are separated by Kyogen comediettas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional format demands a multi-piece, full-day sequence; shorter performances exist for general audiences but do not substitute for the canonical all-day program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement of performers and personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular complement: principal (Shité), assistant (Waki), and a third (Tsuré); chorus (Jiutai) sits in one corner; an orchestra at rear-centre; one or two invisible attendants to assist the principal actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic casting and stage personnel arrangement are required: named roles with precise functions (principal, waki, tsuré), chorus duties akin to Greek chorus, and attendants handling props/costume changes offstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus functions analogous to the Greek chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus sings or chants a considerable portion, sometimes takes theme from the scene or action, gives voice to unuttered thoughts, interprets ideas, gives advice or warning, expresses sympathy, points a moral motif, or impresses religious truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chorus must actively comment, interpret, and moralize; its participation is central to storytelling and to conveying ethical/religious meanings rather than merely providing background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestra composition and strict role division
rubrics_metrics.description: The orchestra is regularly composed of four instruments—a kind of snare-drum at one end and a flute at the other, with two hour-glass shaped drums between—and each of the four is ‘specially played by four respective specialists, each of whom strictly adheres to his own assigned duty.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musicians must observe strict role separation; improvisation across parts is discouraged. Authentic sound and rhythm depend on specialists adhering to assigned duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical function: punctuate tempo and emphasize recitative
rubrics_metrics.description: The instrumental part punctuates the tempo, emphasises the rhythm of the actor’s chant or recitative, and helps to define and increase the emotional values of the entire performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music should keep time with the Shité’s words (often double notes divided into eight parts), include characteristic cries (e.g., ‘yo-hé’), and be used to heighten emotional and temporal structure rather than to ornament indiscriminately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of masks and ritualized motion to represent spirits/ghosts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ghosts stand motionless with white death-masks fixed upon the audience; such mask usage and stylized stillness represent otherworldly states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mask work, immobility, and stylized postures are essential for supernatural characters—evaluation considers the appropriateness of mask type and the controlled stillness/movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/ceremonial origin and didactic moral function
rubrics_metrics.description: Nō was performed by Shintō priests in shrines; texts came from Buddhist priests; performances impress religious truths and superstitions and often present a battle between forces for good and evil over human souls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic Nō conveys spiritual and ethical teachings—evaluations note the balance between religious didacticism and artistic expression (e.g., prayers and priestly intercession as plot devices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on spiritual ideals and training audience imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘supreme regard given by the suggestion of spiritual ideals to a trained and sympathetic imagination’ furnishes controlling artistic principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality is measured by how effectively a production evokes spiritual ideals in the audience’s imagination rather than by literal exposition; audience education/patronage affects reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic conventions may override literal realism (gender and role stylization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylizations (e.g., 'ladies are much respected' so the wife stands in the boat in front of her husband though she would not in real life) reflect theatrical convention overriding realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to traditional theatrical conventions—rather than realistic staging—defines authenticity; departures are noteworthy and affect judgment of fidelity to tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance tempo/style reflecting Bushidō (samurai spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nō-dance, by its deliberate and almost motionless posturing, followed by swift and decisive action, expresses the essence of the Samurai temper and habit (Bushidō).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productions claiming to represent martial or samurai ethos are evaluated on the interplay of stillness and sudden action; rhythm and posture should evoke stoicism and decisive movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interludes and explanatory reciters for popular comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Between acts a man appears and recites in the popular language what has been told in the archaic language of the drama; a popular reciter narrates episodes for the common folk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a reciter or popular-language summaries is an accepted device to make archaic texts accessible; inclusion and quality of these explanations affect audience understanding but should not alter the core performance conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kyogen/farce thematic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Kyogen comediettas commonly depict trials of wits (e.g., scapegrace son vs. doting father), three blind men stealing a Biwa, or sellers of patent medicines—traditional comic themes that provide contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic Kyogen should follow established comic types and rhythms, offering relief and social commentary without undermining the main Nō pieces’ moral seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage, revival, and standards of performance quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Revival and patronage by nobility and literati improved equipment, acting, and audience appreciation; present-day performances (post-Restoration revival) may be judged as exceptionally well performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of modern performances should consider historical continuity, level of patronage/support, and whether production values and interpretive intelligence match or exceed traditional standards.
